'''[[New York City Bus|Bus]]''': {{NYC bus link|Q19|Q69|Q100|M60 SBS}}{{cite NYC bus map|Q}} | embedded = {{Infobox historic site | embed = yes | designation1 = NYCL | designation1_date = June 20, 2006{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|2006|ps=.|p=1}} | designation1_number = 2196 | designation1_free1name = Designated entity | designation1_free1value = Bathhouse facade and pool }} }} '''Astoria Park''' is a {{convert|59.96|acre|ha|sing=on}} public park in the [[Astoria, Queens|Astoria]] neighborhood of [[Queens]] in [[New York City]]. The park is situated on the eastern shore of the [[Hell Gate]], a strait of the [[East River]], between [[Ditmars Boulevard]] to the north and Hoyt Avenue to the south. The [[Robert F. Kennedy Bridge|Robert F. Kennedy (Triborough)]] and [[Hell Gate Bridge]]s respectively pass over the park's southern and northern sections. Astoria Park contains a playground, a soccer field, a running track, a skate park, and courts for tennis, basketball, and [[bocce]]. Astoria Park also includes the '''Astoria Play Center''', which consists of a recreation center and a pool. The park and play center are maintained by the [[New York City Department of Parks and Recreation]] (NYC Parks). Astoria Park was planned in 1905, but the land was not acquired until October 1913. Astoria Park was formally named after the surrounding neighborhood in December 1913, and recreational facilities gradually opened within the park during the next two decades. The pool and bathhouse were designed by John Hatton during a [[Works Progress Administration]] project in 1935–1936 and was used for the [[United States Olympic Trials (swimming)|United States Olympic Trials for swimming]] during 1936, 1952, and 1964. The park was extensively renovated in the 1980s and the late 2010s. The Astoria Play Center was designated a city landmark by the [[New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission]] in 2007. ==Description== Astoria Park is in the [[Astoria, Queens|Astoria]] neighborhood of [[Queens]] in [[New York City]]. It is bounded by Astoria Park South, an extension of Hoyt Avenue, to the south; the [[Hell Gate]], a strait of the [[East River]], to the west; [[Ditmars Boulevard]] to the north; and 19th Street to the east.{{harvnb|Geismar|2017|ps=.|p=1}}{{Cite landmarks|page=632}}{{cite aia5|page=751}} The [[Robert F. Kennedy Bridge|RFK (Triborough) Bridge]] crosses over the southern section of Astoria Park. The [[Hell Gate Bridge]], carrying [[Amtrak]]'s [[Northeast Corridor]] and the [[New York Connecting Railroad]], crosses over the northern section. The park is separated from the Hell Gate and the East River by a {{convert|30|ft|m|-wide|adj=mid|abbr=}} road called Shore Boulevard.{{harvnb|Geismar|2017|ps=.|p=7}} The park covers {{convert|59.96|acre|ha|abbr=}}.{{cite web|title=Astoria Park Highlights|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/astoria-park/history|access-date=January 12, 2021|publisher=New York City Department of Parks and Recreation|archive-date=January 14, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210114060941/https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/astoria-park/history|url-status=live}} The southeastern corner of the park under the RFK Bridge, between Hoyt Avenue North and Hoyt Avenue South, extends east to 21st Street. Astoria Park is crossed by numerous paths, of which some are paved in hexagonal blocks, while others contain asphalt paving. Several paths are built on slopes and contain staggered steps.{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|2006|ps=.|p=14}} Several entrances are spaced around the perimeter of the park.{{harvnb|Geismar|2017|ps=.|p=9}} In the western portion of the park, along Shore Boulevard, is a memorial dedicated to World War I victims.{{cite web|last=|first=|title=Astoria Park War Memorial|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/astoria-park/monuments/59|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210121033455/https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/astoria-park/monuments/59|archive-date=January 21, 2021|access-date=January 14, 2021|website=|publisher=New York City Department of Parks and Recreation}}{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|2006|ps=.|pp=14–15}} There is also a plaque commemorating the [[PS General Slocum|PS ''General Slocum'']],{{cite web|last=Spanos|first=Peter|date=June 16, 2004|title=Honor Death Ship Victims Astoria Park plaque remembers 1904 fire tragedy|url=https://www.nydailynews.com/archives/boroughs/honor-death-ship-victims-astoria-park-plaque-remembers-1904-fire-tragedy-article-1.628641|access-date=January 15, 2021|website=nydailynews.com|archive-date=January 21, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210121014636/https://www.nydailynews.com/archives/boroughs/honor-death-ship-victims-astoria-park-plaque-remembers-1904-fire-tragedy-article-1.628641|url-status=live}} which caught fire and sunk in the Hell Gate in 1904, killing over a thousand people.{{Cite news|last=Kleinfield|first=N. R.|date=September 2, 2007|title=As 9/11 Draws Near, a Debate Rises: How Much Tribute Is Enough?|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url-access=limited|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/09/02/nyregion/02fatigue.html|url-status=live|access-date=January 12, 2021|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=January 14, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210114191409/https://www.nytimes.com/2007/09/02/nyregion/02fatigue.html}} === Recreational facilities === Recreational facilities are concentrated in the southern two-thirds of the park, south of 23rd Avenue.{{cite web|title=Field and Court Usage Report for Astoria Park|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/permits/field-and-court/issued/Q004|access-date=January 15, 2021|publisher=New York City Department of Parks and Recreation|archive-date=January 21, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210121014504/https://www.nycgovparks.org/permits/field-and-court/issued/Q004|url-status=live}} The southernmost portion of Astoria Park, at 18th Street and Astoria Park South, contains a {{Convert|0.25|mi|m|-2|abbr=|adj=on}} running track,{{cite web|title=Astoria Park Running Tracks|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/astoria-park/facilities/runningtracks|access-date=January 15, 2021|publisher=New York City Department of Parks and Recreation|archive-date=January 15, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210115100439/https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/astoria-park/facilities/runningtracks|url-status=live}} which surrounds a soccer field. East of the running track are fourteen tennis courts{{cite web|title=Astoria Park Tennis Courts|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/astoria-park/facilities/tennis|access-date=January 15, 2021|publisher=New York City Department of Parks and Recreation|archive-date=January 16, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210116055147/https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/astoria-park/facilities/tennis|url-status=live}} and a restroom. The tennis court area protrudes slightly under the RFK Bridge. A "tennis landscape" separates the tennis courts from the street. There is a parking lot just north of the running track, underneath the RFK Bridge and at the western end of Hoyt Avenue North. Also underneath the bridge, west of the parking lot, is a {{Convert|21500|ft2||abbr=|adj=on}} skate park.{{cite web|last=Sidman|first=Amanda P.|date=June 5, 2011|title=Best of NY: Astoria Skate Plaza is the best skate park|url=https://www.nydailynews.com/new-york/best-ny-astoria-skate-plaza-best-skate-park-article-1.125017|access-date=January 15, 2021|website=New York Daily News|archive-date=January 20, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210120234448/https://www.nydailynews.com/new-york/best-ny-astoria-skate-plaza-best-skate-park-article-1.125017|url-status=live}}{{cite web|title=Astoria Park Skate Parks|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/astoria-park/facilities/skateparks|access-date=January 15, 2021|publisher=New York City Department of Parks and Recreation|archive-date=January 15, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210115164032/https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/astoria-park/facilities/skateparks|url-status=live}} [[New York Road Runners]] hosts a weekly 3.10-mile Open Run within the park.{{cite web |last=Staff |first=NYRR |date=2023-08-02 |title=Astoria Parksite=NYRR |url=https://www.nyrr.org/openrun/parks/astoria-park |access-date=2023-08-02}} The central portion of the park contains the Astoria Pool and Play Center. There are also basketball courts southwest of the pool area, as well as [[bocce]] courts and Charybdis Playground north of the pool area.{{cite web|title=Astoria Park Bocce Courts|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/astoria-park/facilities/bocce|access-date=January 15, 2021|publisher=New York City Department of Parks and Recreation|archive-date=January 14, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210114204643/https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/astoria-park/facilities/bocce|url-status=live}} Charybdis Playground sits opposite the Hell Gate from Scylla Point on [[Wards Island]]. The two features are named after [[Scylla]] and [[Charybdis]], two water hazards described in Homer's ''[[Odyssey]],''{{cite web|date=April 24, 2017|title=The Top 10 Secrets of Astoria Park in Queens, NYC|url=https://untappedcities.com/2017/04/24/the-top-10-secrets-of-astoria-park-in-queens-nyc/|access-date=January 12, 2021|website=Untapped New York|archive-date=January 14, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210114115749/https://untappedcities.com/2017/04/24/the-top-10-secrets-of-astoria-park-in-queens-nyc/|url-status=live}} and refer to the dangerous whirlpools in the waters of the Hell Gate.{{Cite news|last=Pollak|first=Michael|date=2008-06-29|title=Turning Away Wrath|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url-access=limited|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/06/29/nyregion/thecity/29fyi.html|access-date=2021-01-15|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=December 9, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171209044106/http://www.nytimes.com/2008/06/29/nyregion/thecity/29fyi.html|url-status=live}} Charybdis Playground was named first, in 1997; Scylla Point was named in 2001 after parks commissioner [[Henry Stern (New York politician)|Henry Stern]] petitioned the federal government to rename what was then known as "Negro Point", in 2001.{{Cite news|last=Baard|first=Erik|date=July 8, 2001|title=Neighborhood Report: Wards Island; Uneasily Evoking an Outdated Past|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url-access=limited|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2001/07/08/nyregion/neighborhood-report-wards-island-uneasily-evoking-an-outdated-past.html|url-status=live|access-date=January 15, 2021|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=January 22, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210122060202/https://www.nytimes.com/2001/07/08/nyregion/neighborhood-report-wards-island-uneasily-evoking-an-outdated-past.html}} Charybdis Playground contains a decorated one-story brick restroom. The restroom contains decorative [[Pier (architecture)|piers]] protruding from all four corners; glass-block openings; and Art Deco lettering indicating the girls' and boys' restrooms.{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|2006|ps=.|p=15}} ===Astoria Play Center=== ====Pools==== [[File:Astoria Park pool, Queens NYC.jpg|thumb|View of the main pool|alt=View of the main pool with the Hell Gate Bridge in the background]] Astoria Park contains an enclosed elliptical pool area that is aligned north-south, with two pools (formerly three).{{cite web|title=Astoria Park Diving Pool Plaza Construction|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/planning-and-building/capital-project-tracker/project/5960|access-date=January 14, 2021|publisher=New York City Department of Parks and Recreation|archive-date=January 21, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210121035824/https://www.nycgovparks.org/planning-and-building/capital-project-tracker/project/5960|url-status=live}} The main pool is rectangular and measures {{Convert|330|by|165|ft|abbr=}},{{cite web|title=Astoria Park Outdoor Pools|url=http://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/AstoriaPark/facilities/pools|access-date=January 14, 2021|publisher=New York City Department of Parks and Recreation|archive-date=May 22, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130522134559/http://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/AstoriaPark/facilities/pools|url-status=live}}{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/67847266/|title=Taking the plunge|first=Lisa|last=Rein|date=1999-06-30|work=New York Daily News|access-date=2021-01-17|page=164|via=newspapers.com {{open access}}|archive-date=May 9, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220509134450/https://www.newspapers.com/clip/67847266/taking-the-plunge/|url-status=live}} with a depth of {{convert|4|ft}} and a surface area of {{convert|54450|ft2|m2|abbr=}}. It was the largest of 11 pools in New York City that were completed by the [[Works Progress Administration]] in 1936.{{cite news|date=September 27, 1937|title=City Projects Gain by Huge Federal Aid|page=22|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/67638928/|access-date=January 15, 2021|via=newspapers.com {{open access}}|archive-date=May 10, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220510125637/https://www.newspapers.com/clip/67638928/city-projects-gain-by-huge-federal-aid/|url-status=live}} At its peak, the pool area was able to fit 6,200 swimmers,{{Cite news|last=Smith|first=Sarah Harrison|date=July 12, 2013|title=Pool Built for the People, 6,200 at a Time|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url-access=limited|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2013/07/14/nyregion/pool-built-for-the-people-6200-at-a-time.html|url-status=live|access-date=January 14, 2021|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=January 21, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210121033450/https://www.nytimes.com/2013/07/14/nyregion/pool-built-for-the-people-6200-at-a-time.html}}{{harvnb|Robins|2017|pp=225–226|ps=.}} and the main pool alone had a capacity of 5,570. The pools hosted [[United States Olympic Trials (swimming)|swimming trials]] for three [[Summer Olympic Games]] in [[1936 Summer Olympics|1936]], [[1952 Summer Olympics|1952]], and [[1964 Summer Olympics|1964]].{{cite web|last=Evelly|first=Jeanmarie|date=August 23, 2016|title=Reopen Astoria Diving Pool Instead of Turning It Into Event Space: Petition|url=https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20160823/ditmars/reopen-astoria-diving-pool-instead-of-turning-it-into-event-space-petition|access-date=January 14, 2021|website=DNAinfo New York|archive-date=January 28, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210128022823/https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20160823/ditmars/reopen-astoria-diving-pool-instead-of-turning-it-into-event-space-petition/|url-status=dead}} The main pool is flanked by two semicircular pools, each with a 165-foot diameter.{{cite news|date=July 3, 1936|title=Hopkins, Mayor Dedicate Pool Before 40,000: 'If This Is Boondoggling, I'd Like to See More of It,' Says W. P. A. Chief Moses and Ridder Speak Asloria Plant Biggest of 12 Constructed in Parks|page=10|work=New York Herald Tribune|url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/1237413632|url-access=subscription|access-date=January 15, 2021|id={{ProQuest|1237413632}}}} The wading pool is north of the main pool and is surrounded by spray spouts. The diving pool to the south was drained and fenced off in the 1980s, and was totally infilled between 2017 and 2019. The still-extant diving board measures {{Convert|32|ft||abbr=}} tall,{{cite news|last=Hanc|first=John|date=March 24, 2002|title=Queens Life Outdoors / Parks / a Patch of Sanity / Astoria Park Gives Queens Residents an Oasis as the World Passes by Overhead|page=G08|work=Newsday|url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/279517481|url-access=subscription|access-date=January 15, 2021|id={{ProQuest|279517481}}}}{{cite web|date=September 14, 2016|title=Resident's plea for the restoration of Astoria Park Diving Pool gets cool reception from Parks Dept.|url=https://astoriapost.com/residents-plea-for-the-restoration-of-astoria-park-diving-pool-gets-cool-reception-from-parks-dept|access-date=January 14, 2021|website=Astoria Post|archive-date=January 21, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210121033713/https://astoriapost.com/residents-plea-for-the-restoration-of-astoria-park-diving-pool-gets-cool-reception-from-parks-dept|url-status=live}} with three platforms cantilevered over each other.{{cite news|date=April 12, 1936|title=Moses Shows a Model of Astoria Pool Tower|page=2|work=New York Herald Tribune|url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/1329990347|url-access=subscription|access-date=January 15, 2021|id={{ProQuest|1329990347}}}} The diving board, described by ''[[Architectural Record]]'' as "an example of design for function",{{Cite magazine|last=|first=|date=April 1941|title=Swimming Pools|url=https://usmodernist.org/AR/AR-1941-04.pdf|magazine=Architectural Record|volume=|pages=93|via=|access-date=January 15, 2021|archive-date=July 19, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200719110608/https://usmodernist.org/AR/AR-1941-04.pdf|url-status=live}} allowed four contestants to dive simultaneously: one each from the top and bottom, and two from the middle. The deck surrounding the pools is made of cement. The deck is surrounded by concrete bleachers and enclosed by a brick perimeter wall topped by a wrought iron fence.{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|2006|ps=.|pp=13–14}} There is also a filter house on the western side of the pool area. The filter house contains a balcony that is raised one story above the pool deck and two stories above a plaza to the west. The filter house's balcony has a roof that is designed like a saucer. ====Bathhouse==== [[File:Astoria Pool jeh.jpg|thumb|The bathhouse as seen from the pool|alt=The main pool with the bathhouse in the background]] The bathhouse was designed by John Hatton.{{harvnb|Robins|2017|p=226|ps=.}} It incorporates both classical motifs, such as brick piers, and modern motifs, such as geometric brickwork. The bathhouse is a U-shaped brick structure west of 19th Street, between 23rd Drive to the north and 23rd Terrace to the south. Pavilions extend north and south of the bathhouse's central lobby. Wings extend eastward into the hillside from the ends of both pavilions. The main entrance plaza is sunken below street level, surrounded by the bathhouse pavilion to the west, the wings to the north and south, and 19th Street to the east. The entrance plaza is accessed via two ramps with steps, which extend north to 23rd Drive and south to 23rd Terrace.{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|2006|ps=.|p=11}} The main entrance is flanked by a pair of stepped-brick piers with [[glass brick]] columns set into the middle of each pier. The pool entrance, at the center of the western facade, is also flanked by stepped-brick piers with glass brick columns and contains a clock suspended above the center. As designed, the pool entrance was flanked by two stainless steel sculptures created by [[Emil Siebern]], which depicted female athletes.{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|2006|ps=.|p=10}}{{Cite press release|title=Two identical statues of stainless steel will be erected in the near future on the promenade of the Astoria swimming Pool in the Borough of Queens.|date=April 18, 1936|publisher=New York City Department of Parks and Recreation|access-date=January 6, 2021|url=http://nyc.gov/html/records/pdf/govpub/41891936_press_releases.pdf|at=PDF p. 65|archive-date=January 8, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210108041415/http://nyc.gov/html/records/pdf/govpub/41891936_press_releases.pdf|url-status=live}} The lobby between the main and pool entrances is open to the outdoors and contains a brick floor surrounded by bluestone and granite. The ceiling of the lobby contains concrete beams. The octagonal ticket booth at the center of the lobby has a nautical theme, with an outwardly angled terrazzo base, a ticket collector's cage, and a ventilation [[cupola]] on the roof. The north and south walls are divided into three bays and contain the women's and men's locker rooms. These bays contain glass bricks at the top and openings or doorways at the bottom. Above the center bays on each side are [[Art Deco]]-style aluminum letters indicating the respective genders' locker rooms. The bathhouse pavilions are similar in design. The east facade is fifteen bays wide, while the west facade is seventeen bays wide. Except for the central bay on each side, there are openings with glass blocks topped by metal louvers; these are separated by fluted brick piers. At the northern and southern ends of the west facade, there are semicircular coves with doorways that lead to the bathhouse's locker rooms. The eastern wings of the bathhouse, to the north and south of the entrance court, each contain two bays of horizontal glass-brick bands.{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|2006|ps=.|pp=12–13}} The roof of the bathhouse pavilion doubles as a viewing platform and contains a concrete deck and metal railing. The eastern portion of the roof is higher than the western portion. The roof contains two concrete ventilators above the main entrance.{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|2006|ps=.|p=13}} Upon the bathhouse's completion, ''[[Architectural Forum]]'' praised its use of glass bricks "for privacy and ease of maintenance".{{Cite magazine|last=|first=|date=August 1927|title=Pavilion; Astoria Swimming Pool, New York|url=https://usmodernist.org/AF/AF-1937-08.pdf|magazine=Architectural Forum|volume=|pages=127|via=|access-date=January 15, 2021|archive-date=July 31, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200731152000/https://usmodernist.org/AF/AF-1937-08.pdf|url-status=live}} ==History== The park site formerly contained Pot Cove, a [[Native Americans in the United States|Native American]] settlement used for maize cultivation and fishing.{{cite book|last1=LaRose|first1=M.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fI-gsoO63MYC&pg=PA13|title=Long Island City|last2=Society|first2=G.A.H.|last3=Leone|first3=S.|last4=Melnick|first4=R.|publisher=Arcadia Pub.|year=2007|isbn=978-0-7385-5543-0|series=Postcard history series|page=13|access-date=January 12, 2021|archive-date=May 10, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220510125632/https://books.google.com/books?id=fI-gsoO63MYC&pg=PA13|url-status=live}} The name also applies to the small cove next to the park's southwestern corner.{{cite web|last=Marzlock|first=Ron|date=February 20, 2014|title=Spectacular views in Astoria Park|url=https://www.qchron.com/qboro/i_have_often_walked/spectacular-views-in-astoria-park/article_ffeb5ca2-d1d4-5371-b3a0-25cd2a1a280f.html|access-date=January 12, 2021|website=Queens Chronicle|archive-date=January 14, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210114101310/https://www.qchron.com/qboro/i_have_often_walked/spectacular-views-in-astoria-park/article_ffeb5ca2-d1d4-5371-b3a0-25cd2a1a280f.html|url-status=live}} The settlement's namesake may have been the {{Convert|130|ft||-long|abbr=|adj=mid}} Pot Rock within the Hell Gate; the rock was dynamited in 1876 as part of the [[removal of Hell Gate rocks]].{{harvnb|Geismar|2017|ps=.|p=10}}{{Cite web|last=Bergoffen|first=Celia|date=July 9, 2013|title=Phase IA Archaeological Assessment, Astoria Cove, Block 906, lot 1, Block 908, lot 12, and Block 909, Lot 35, Borough of Queens, New York|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/applicants/env-review/astoria_cove/appendd_feis.pdf|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210114103732/https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/applicants/env-review/astoria_cove/appendd_feis.pdf|archive-date=January 14, 2021|access-date=January 12, 2021|website=|publisher=[[New York City Department of City Planning]]|pages=7–8}} There were hills immediately above the Hell Gate shoreline, and several creeks emptied into the cove. One of these was Linden Brook, which flowed along the current path of Astoria Park South and into Pot Cove.{{cite web|title=Linden Brook, Queens|url=https://watercourses.typepad.com/watercourses/2008/09/linden-brook-queens.html|access-date=January 12, 2021|website=Watercourses|archive-date=January 15, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210115145758/https://watercourses.typepad.com/watercourses/2008/09/linden-brook-queens.html|url-status=live}} The surrounding land had numerous owners from the 17th to 19th centuries. The tracts were developed with the estates of wealthy businessmen such as Edwin Hoyt, Edward Woolsey, and Henry Barclay. Maps show that some streets had already been laid out on the future park site by the late 19th century.{{harvnb|Geismar|2017|ps=.|p=13}} The surrounding Astoria neighborhood was part of the independent city of [[Long Island City]], which was combined into the [[City of Greater New York]] in 1898.{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|2006|ps=.|p=3}} [[Augustus D. La Guardia]] nominated [[Robert Moses]] to become commissioner of a unified [[New York City Department of Parks and Recreation]]. At the time, the United States was experiencing the [[Great Depression]]; immediately after La Guardia won the [[1933 New York City mayoral election|1933 election]], Moses began to write "a plan for putting 80,000 men to work on 1,700 relief projects".{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|2006|ps=.|pp=4–5}}{{harvnb|ps=.|Rodgers|1952|p=82}} By the time he was in office, several hundred such projects were underway across the city.{{harvnb|ps=.|Rodgers|1952|p=84}} Moses was especially interested in creating new pools and other bathing facilities, such as those in [[Jacob Riis Park]], [[Jones Beach State Park|Jones Beach]], and [[Orchard Beach (Bronx)|Orchard Beach]].{{Caro: The Power Broker|page=456}}{{Stern: New York|page=717|edition=1930}} He devised a list of 23 pools around the city, including one at Astoria Park.{{Cite news|date=July 23, 1934|title=23 Bathing Pools Planned by Moses; Nine to Be Begun in a Month to Meet Shortage of Facilities Caused by Pollution|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url-access=subscription|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1934/07/23/archives/23-bathing-pools-planned-by-moses-nine-to-be-begun-in-a-month-to.html|access-date=August 9, 2019|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=August 9, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190809035319/https://www.nytimes.com/1934/07/23/archives/23-bathing-pools-planned-by-moses-nine-to-be-begun-in-a-month-to.html|url-status=live}}{{Cite press release|title=Public Swimming Facilities in New York City.|date=July 23, 1934|publisher=New York City Department of Parks and Recreation|access-date=January 6, 2021|page=3 (PDF p. 30)|url=http://nyc.gov/html/records/pdf/govpub/41861934_press_releases_part1.pdf|archive-date=January 8, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210108104839/http://nyc.gov/html/records/pdf/govpub/41861934_press_releases_part1.pdf|url-status=live}} The pools would be built using funds from the [[Works Progress Administration]] (WPA), a federal agency created as part of the [[New Deal]] to combat the Depression's negative effects.{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/35042789/|title=City to Construct 9 Pools To Provide Safe Swimming|date=July 23, 1934|work=New York Daily News|access-date=August 18, 2019|page=8|via=newspapers.com {{open access}}|archive-date=May 9, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220509134446/https://www.newspapers.com/clip/35042789/city-to-construct-9-pools-to-provide/|url-status=live}} Eleven of these pools were to be designed concurrently and open in 1936. Moses, along with the architects [[Aymar Embury II]] and [[Gilmore David Clarke]], created a common design for these proposed aquatic centers. Each location was to have distinct pools for diving, swimming, and wading; bleachers and viewing areas; and bathhouses with locker rooms that could be used as gymnasiums. The pools were to have several common features, such as a minimum {{Convert|55|yd|m|abbr=|adj=on}} length, underwater lighting, heating, and filtration, all constructed using inexpensive materials. To fit the requirement for efficiency and low-cost construction, each building would be built using elements of the [[Streamline Moderne]] and [[Classical architecture|Classical]] architectural styles. The buildings would also be near "comfort stations", additional playgrounds, and spruced-up landscapes.{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|2006|ps=.|pp=8–9}}{{Cite news|last=Shattuck|first=Kathryn|date=August 14, 2006|title=Big Chill of '36: Show Celebrates Giant Depression-Era Pools That Cool New York|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url-access=limited|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2006/08/14/arts/design/big-chill-of-36-show-celebrates-giant-depressionera-pools-that.html|url-status=live|access-date=January 8, 2021|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=January 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210110031731/https://www.nytimes.com/2006/08/14/arts/design/big-chill-of-36-show-celebrates-giant-depressionera-pools-that.html}}{{cite web | title=History of Parks' Swimming Pools | publisher=New York City Department of Parks and Recreation | url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/about/history/pools | access-date=2021-01-15 | archive-date=January 17, 2021 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210117002610/https://www.nycgovparks.org/about/history/pools | url-status=live }} Construction for some of the 11 pools began in October 1934.{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|2006|ps=.|p=9}}{{Cite news|last=|first=|date=October 4, 1934|title=Park Work Is Begun on 2 Bathing Pools; Construction Under Way at High Bridge and Hamilton Fish – 7 Others to Be Started Soon|language=en-US|page=48|work=The New York Times|url-access=subscription|url=http://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1934/10/04/93645601.pdf|url-status=live|access-date=January 13, 2021|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=May 9, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220509134446/http://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1934/10/04/93645601.html?pdf_redirect=true&site=false}} The excavation plan for a large pool complex at Astoria Park was issued that December, to replace the existing wading pool. Moses was also planning a "model playground" at Astoria Park, one of five around the city.{{cite news|date=February 10, 1934|title=Moses Planning 5 Playgrounds As City Models: Shade Trees, Night Lights, Possibly fading Pools. to improve Barren Lots Each Borough Gets One Fun for Adults as Well as, Children To Be Provided|page=7|work=New York Herald Tribune|url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/1242987942|url-access=subscription|access-date=January 15, 2021|id={{ProQuest|1242987942}}}} The complex was initially supposed to be completed by mid-1935,{{cite news|date=April 4, 1935|title=Astoria Park Bathing Pool Work Speeded|page=473|work=New York Daily News|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/67571512/|access-date=January 15, 2021|via=newspapers.com {{open access}}}} but this was delayed due to a temporary work stoppage.{{cite news|date=July 9, 1935|title=City Resumes Building of Astoria Park Pool|page=383|work=New York Daily News|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/67571749/|access-date=January 15, 2021|via=newspapers.com {{open access}}}} Plans for the bathhouse, landscape, bleachers, and filter house were completed by the end of 1935. John Hatton was responsible for the pool complex's primary design, while Gregory Kiely designed some minor details. The war memorial was moved to make way for the pool. By mid-1936, ten of the eleven WPA-funded pools were completed and were being opened at a rate of one per week.
